hapless

HAP-lis -- from Middle English hap ('luck, chance,' from Old Norse happ) + -less ('without'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Hapless is unfortunate, dogged by bad luck the person did nothing to deserve.

The hapless intern spilled coffee on the CEO twice in the same week, purely by rotten luck.

Example

A tourist misses his flight, then loses his passport, then gets caught in a sudden downpour, all in the same afternoon, without doing anything to deserve any of it.

That string of pure, undeserved bad luck -- one misfortune piling onto the next -- is exactly what hapless describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

luckless: Luckless means exactly what it says -- without luck -- and it states the misfortune plainly, as a flat fact. Hapless says nearly the same thing with a tone of gentle pity and a literary, storytelling flavor: the hapless hero of a comedy stumbles from mishap to mishap while the audience winces for him.

jinxed: Jinxed is the playful, superstitious cousin of hapless -- a jinxed player blames a hex or a broken charm for a losing streak, usually over something as small as a game. Hapless makes no claim about magic: it simply describes someone dogged by undeserved bad luck, with gentle pity attached.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fortunate: having good luck

charmed: protected by extraordinary good fortune, as if by magic

Where it sits · how relentless the misfortune is — unlucky → hapless → cursed

unlucky vs. hapless: Unlucky is the plainer, everyday version of hapless -- almost anyone having one bad day can be called unlucky, while hapless often implies an ongoing pattern of misfortune, sometimes with a hint of gentle pity.

cursed vs. hapless: Cursed pushes far beyond hapless -- a hapless person is dogged by ordinary, undeserved bad luck, while cursed suggests misfortune so relentless and total that it feels supernatural, as if fate itself had singled the victim out.

Put it together

Put it together: Hapless comes from Middle English hap ('luck, chance,' borrowed from Old Norse happ) plus the suffix -less ('without') -- so someone hapless is, quite literally, 'without luck,' at the mercy of one misfortune after another.

Word Choice

Hapless usually carries a note of gentle pity rather than blame -- a hapless character's misfortunes are almost always due to bad luck, not their own poor choices, unlike a word such as careless.
